title: Project Overview
description: CasesTD is a Bloons-style tower defense game with a case-opening (gacha) layer: you earn Coins by clearing zombie waves, open cases to unbox towers into an inventory, then place, upgrade, or sell them. The README covers setup (JDK 21, Maven, MySQL 8, running schema.sql and seed_data.sql, copying the DB config) and GAME_GUIDE.md is the defense guide that maps the layered architecture and shows where each OOP concept lives. Read both first, because the rest of the tour follows the same layers: database, domain model, game core, and Swing UI.

title: Build and Entry Point
description: pom.xml is the Maven build for Java 21, and it pulls in MySQL Connector/J and Gson, the two libraries the persistence and config layers use. Main.java is the entry point. On the Swing event thread it creates the fixed-size MainFrame (a CardLayout that hosts every screen) and wires in AppController, which switches between the landing, game, and results screens. The BFS dependency walk starts here, and every other class is reached through AppController.
languageLesson: Swing is not thread-safe, so the UI must be built on the Event Dispatch Thread. SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() -> ...) schedules the lambda on the EDT. CardLayout stacks several panels in one container and shows one at a time, which is a simple way to build screen navigation.

title: Database Schema and Seed Data
description: The MySQL schema splits the data into two groups. The rebuildable catalog tables are towers (class, rarity, damage, range, fire rate, special effect), cases (cost plus per-rarity drop weights constrained to sum to 100), and the case_towers join table that defines each case's drop pool. The players table is persistent and stores each profile's best score. seed_data.sql fills in the starting tower catalog and the Standard/Premium/Legendary cases, so balancing is data-driven: tower and case stats live in the database, not in Java code.
languageLesson: case_towers is a classic many-to-many join table: one case can drop many towers, and one tower can appear in many cases. Its foreign keys use ON DELETE CASCADE so join rows are removed with their parent. A CHECK constraint (weights summing to 100) enforces a business rule in the database itself.

title: Singleton Database Connection
description: DatabaseConnection is the project's Singleton: a lazily created single instance reads the JDBC URL, user, and password from data/db_config.properties (git-ignored, copied from the example template) and hands out the one shared connection. Keeping credentials in a properties file keeps secrets out of source control, and the Singleton gives every DAO in the next step the same access point.
languageLesson: Singleton pattern in Java: a private constructor stops outside code from calling new, a private static field holds the one instance, and a public static getInstance() creates it on first use (lazy initialization). Be ready to explain the trade-off: it is a global access point, which is convenient but makes testing harder.

title: DAO Layer
description: The DAO (Data Access Object) pattern keeps all SQL in the dao package. TowerDAO maps rows of the towers table to TowerType records, CaseDAO joins cases with case_towers to build CaseDef records, and PlayerDAO looks up, creates, and updates Player profiles and their high scores. The rest of the game never sees SQL or JDBC. It works with plain Java objects, which is a clear example of separation of concerns.
languageLesson: JDBC basics: get a Connection, build a PreparedStatement (the ? placeholders prevent SQL injection), and iterate a ResultSet with rs.next(). try-with-resources (try (var ps = ...) { }) closes statements and result sets automatically, even when an exception is thrown.

title: Type Object: Blueprints and Catalog
description: TowerType is the single most depended-on file (highest fan-in). It is an immutable blueprint for one tower row: name, class, Rarity, base stats, and Special effect. It is not a tower on the map. That is the Type Object pattern: many placed Tower objects (Step 7) can share one TowerType. CaseDef plays the same role for cases, and Catalog loads every TowerType and CaseDef once at startup through the DAOs and keeps them in memory, so gameplay never queries the database.
languageLesson: Java records (record TowerType(String name, ...)) are concise immutable data carriers: the compiler generates the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString. Java enums like Rarity can hold fields and constructors (display name, color, gem count), so they are full classes with a fixed set of instances.

title: Tower: Template Method and Interfaces
description: Tower is the abstract base of every placed tower and implements the Template Method pattern. Its final update() handles cooldown timing and then calls the abstract attack() hook that each subclass must provide, so the overall algorithm is fixed and only the targeting and damage step varies. Tower also implements the Upgradable interface (level reads and level-ups), and UpgradeCostTable says how many duplicate copies an upgrade costs for each rarity, which ties the gacha inventory into upgrades.
languageLesson: Declaring update() as final stops subclasses from overriding the skeleton. Declaring attack() as abstract forces them to fill in the step. Abstract class vs interface: Tower holds shared state and code (abstract class), while Upgradable is only a contract (interface). A class can extend one class but implement many interfaces.

title: Tower Subclasses and Polymorphism
description: Each concrete tower overrides the attack() hook from Step 7 differently. SingleTargetTower shoots the enemy furthest along the track, SniperTower picks the highest-health enemy and can fire a piercing beam, SplashTower deals area damage with poison or burn, and SupportTower changes behavior based on its Special (stun, turrets, buffs). The engine just calls tower.update() on a list of Tower references, and dynamic dispatch runs the right subclass code. That is runtime polymorphism.
languageLesson: @Override asks the compiler to check that a method really overrides a superclass method. Polymorphism means the declared type (Tower) decides which methods you can call, and the runtime object type (SniperTower) decides which implementation runs.

title: Enemy Hierarchy and Hooks
description: Enemy is the abstract zombie base class and implements the Damageable interface. It handles movement along the path, health, rewards, and status effects such as stun with immunity windows. Subclasses specialize through overriding: ArmoredEnemy overrides the reduceDamage hook to take 30% less damage, BossEnemy (every 10th wave) halves any stun applied to it, and FastEnemy trades health for speed. Towers from Step 8 only ever talk to the Enemy/Damageable type, so new zombie kinds need no tower changes.
languageLesson: A protected hook method like reduceDamage(double dmg) gives subclasses one specific point to change behavior without copying the base class's takeDamage logic. Overriding it in ArmoredEnemy is a small, clear polymorphism example to show a professor. The base class calls the hook, the subclass decides the result.

title: Factory Pattern
description: TowerFactory maps a TowerType's tower_class string from the database to the matching concrete Tower subclass. EnemyFactory turns an enemy type name into the right Enemy subclass and applies the wave's health and speed scaling. Callers ask for a tower or enemy by data, never by calling new SniperTower(...) directly, so object creation lives in one place. This is how database rows (Step 3) become polymorphic objects (Steps 8 and 9).
languageLesson: A Java switch expression (switch (cls) { case "SNIPER" -> new SniperTower(type); ... default -> throw ...; }) is a clean way to write a simple factory. The return type is the abstract base class, so callers depend on the abstraction, not on concrete classes.

title: Map Path and Distance Movement
description: GameMap loads the zombie path from map1_path.csv as a polyline of x,y corner points and describes positions by distance traveled along the path, not by raw coordinates. An enemy only stores how far it has walked, and GameMap converts that distance into a screen point by finding the right segment and interpolating within it. It also decides where towers may be placed. The same distance value lets towers find the enemy furthest along the track.
languageLesson: Linear interpolation: for a segment from A to B of length len, a point at distance d into it is A + (B - A) * (d / len). Precomputing cumulative segment lengths turns 'where is distance X?' into a quick lookup.

title: Waves and Game Balance Config
description: waves_config.json holds all the tuning numbers: starting coins and lives, wave rewards, kill coins, sell refunds, wave scaling, and explicit spawn lists for the early waves. GameConfig is the Gson-deserialized Java view of that file. WaveSpawner uses it to build a time-stamped spawn queue for each wave, falling back to a formula for later waves and adding a boss every 10th wave, and EnemyFactory (Step 10) creates the actual enemies. Designers can rebalance the game without recompiling.
languageLesson: Gson maps JSON to Java objects by reflection: new Gson().fromJson(reader, GameConfig.class) fills fields whose names match the JSON keys, including nested objects and lists. A spawn queue sorted by timestamp lets the engine release each enemy once elapsed time passes its spawn time.

title: Game Engine and Fixed-Timestep Loop
description: GamePanel is the main gameplay screen and the widest-reaching file (highest fan-out). It runs a fixed-timestep loop: a time accumulator advances the simulation in exact 1/60 s steps, multiplied for the x1/x2/x3 speed buttons and paused while the shop is open. Each tick calls GameEngine, which runs the wave, recomputes tower buffs, fires towers, moves enemies, and pays kill and wave rewards. VisualEffect objects (shot lines, blast circles) fade out over time. Keeping the simulation in GameEngine and the drawing in GamePanel separates model from view.
languageLesson: Fixed timestep: accumulator += frameTime; while (accumulator >= DT) { update(DT); accumulator -= DT; } then repaint(). Physics stays deterministic no matter how fast frames render. In Swing, drawing goes in an overridden paintComponent(Graphics g), and you trigger it with repaint(), never by calling paint directly.

title: Session Economy and Gacha RNG
description: GameSession holds the state for one run (coins, lives, free cases, inventory copies, placed towers) and is the project's clearest encapsulation example. Fields are private, and the only way to change them is through methods that enforce the rules, such as being unable to buy a case without enough coins or upgrade without enough copies. CaseRNGManager does the gacha roll: it first picks a rarity from the case's weighted odds, then picks a tower of that rarity from the case's pool. ShopOverlay is the UI on top, showing case cards with drop odds and the unboxing animation.
languageLesson: Weighted random choice: draw r = random.nextInt(totalWeight), then walk the options subtracting each weight until r < weight. With weights summing to 100, each weight is the percentage chance. Encapsulation means methods like trySpendCoins(int) return success or failure instead of exposing a public setter, so invalid states cannot happen.

title: Screens and Run Lifecycle
description: The remaining screens complete the player's journey that AppController (Step 2) manages. LandingPanel takes the player name and loads or creates the profile through PlayerDAO, SidePanel shows inventory cards and selected-tower info during play, and ResultsPanel shows the immutable RunResult (waves cleared, kills, cases opened, new-record flag) before PLAY AGAIN. That full loop (login, play, unbox, results, save high score) uses every layer of the tour, so it is a good way to finish a demo.
